findings.title: Queries are now interpolated twice (ad hoc filters applied twice) per sub-request
findings.body: `runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` up-front, but the sub-requests built from these targets are still executed with `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)`, and `runQuery` delegates to `DataSourceWithBackend.query()`, which maps every target through `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` again (the sub-request keeps `scopedVars` and `filters` from the original request). Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent in one respect: it calls `addAdHocFilters(target.expr, adhocFilters)`, so the same ad hoc filters are injected a second time into an expression that already contains them, yielding duplicated matchers/label filters (e.g. `{a="b", env="prod", env="prod"}` or a repeated `| env="prod"`). Variable values are also substituted twice, so any value that itself contains `$name`/`${name}` will be expanded on the second pass. Either strip `filters`/`scopedVars` from the sub-requests, or keep interpolation in a single place.

findings.title: Shard path interpolates each query three times and changes the selector used to fetch shard values
findings.body: `runShardSplitQuery` now interpolates targets with `applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`; the resulting sharded sub-request is then handed to `runSplitQuery()`, which (after this PR) interpolates again, and finally `datasource.runQuery()` -> `DataSourceWithBackend.query()` interpolates a third time. Since Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` re-runs `addAdHocFilters`, each pass re-inserts the same ad hoc filters into the already sharded expression, producing duplicated matchers. Additionally, the previous code called `interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars)` without ad hoc filters, whereas the new call passes `request.filters`; the selector derived by `getSelectorForShardValues()` and sent to `fetchLabelValues('__stream_shard__', { streamSelector })` now includes ad hoc filters, which silently changes which shard values are discovered. This behaviour change is untested.

findings.title: Test encodes repeated interpolation (5 calls for 1 target) as expected behaviour
findings.body: The assertion was changed from `interpolateVariablesInQueries` being called once to `applyTemplateVariables` being called 5 times for a single target. Those 5 calls are 1 call in `runShardSplitQuery` plus 1 per shard sub-request from the newly added interpolation inside `runSplitQuery`; i.e. the test now locks in the duplicate interpolation of each sub-request. It only passes because the mock at line 56 mutates the query object and does a plain `replace('$SELECTOR', ...)`, which is a no-op on the second pass; a realistic mock (returning a copy and re-applying ad hoc filters) would show duplicated filters. The mock also mutates its input, unlike the real `applyTemplateVariables`, which returns a new object, so target mutation regressions cannot be caught here.

findings.title: New interpolation test mocks replace() in a way that contradicts real `$__auto` handling
findings.body: The test's `replace` mock substitutes `$__auto` with `5m`, and the test then asserts the executed expr is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. Loki's real `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately removes `__auto`, `__interval`, `__range` (and their variants) from `scopedVars` so that they are interpolated on the backend with the *split* time range; a real `templateSrv.replace` would leave `$__auto` untouched here. The test therefore asserts behaviour that does not occur in production and would not catch a regression where `$__auto` is prematurely resolved against the full range. Using a non-range variable (like the `$step` part of the test) or a real templateSrv stub with defined variables would make the test meaningful.
